blocks.text: Classical India is easily misunderstood if enduring political unity is treated as the only measure of civilizational maturity. Governments and centers could change while language, religion, knowledge and social organization circulated through multiple institutions and communities. Continuity was not stored only in the state.

Mauryan and Gupta arrangements differed in political scale and conditions. They should not be presented as an unchanged institutional line. The more revealing question is which connections sustained a common civilizational space as political forms changed.

blocks.caption: Gupta and Post-Gupta South Asia · Context illustration; historical interpretation is in the text.

blocks.text: The Maya world likewise challenges the assumption of a single center. Urban networks, knowledge and political competition could together sustain complexity. Multiple centers did not simply indicate societies waiting for a unified state that had not yet arrived.

India and Maya did not thereby become one kind of civilization. Their juxtaposition asks a narrower question: what carries complexity and continuity beyond political unity? The answer must preserve their distinct environments, periods and evidential limits.
